messages.subject: Model Identification and Sample Size
parts:
Dear colleagues, 

I am a student and  new to SEM and going to conduct analysis, but I doubt whether my sample size is OK. 
Is it possible to conduct SEM if my sample size is 200 (with some missings) and the number of items is 150 with 6 factors. or there are too many parametres ? 

Thank you in advance

messages.author: f6d12b388faad456
messages.subject: Re: Model Identification and Sample Size
parts:
By my experience, the more items you have, the smaller the sample needs to be, and 200 should be enough.
However, I've never tried a model with 150 items. Have you tried any analysis so far? Did some error occur?

Best,
Yago

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Model Identification and Sample Size
parts: If a model with 150 observed variables loading on 6 factors is conventionally specified, there would be more than 300 parameters to estimate from only 200 incomplete observations. I would expect that instability in the covariance matrix of the 150 observed variables--a matrix with 11,325 distinct elements.--would be so great that it would be risky to infer anything from the results. It is impressive that you have an average of 150 / 6 = 25 observed variables per common factor. My guess is that you could put more confidence in results from summing the (standardized) indicators to form 6 composites.

messages.author: bfa43814f6ba1969
messages.subject: Re: Model Identification and Sample Size
parts:
Hi,

 

That will occur when the number of parameters exceeds the sample size. Note that the problem is not about the number of indicators per se, but about the number of parameters that you estimate.

 

Parceling will reduce the number of parameters and will help with the problem. Another thing that you can do is to estimate each factor separately and then fix the loadings and error variances to those estimates when you run the full model.

 

What did you run the det() and eigen() functions on? The sample covariance matrix or the variance-covariance matrix of the estimates?

 

Mikko

messages.author: bfa43814f6ba1969
messages.subject: Re: Model Identification and Sample Size
parts:
Hi,

 

The error is about the variance-covariance matrix of estimates, not sample covariance matrix. If your sample covariance matrix is not positive definite, most SEM estimators cannot even give you estimates. If you want to check with det() and eigen() you can check the VCOV that Lavaan provides.

 

Changing the estimator will not help with this problem. Only reducing the estimated parameters will.

 

If you have many indicators, going with MLR is a safe bet in most situations. See

 

Rhemtulla, M., Brosseau-Liard, P. É., & Savalei, V. (2012). When can categorical variables be treated as continuous? A comparison of robust continuous and categorical SEM estimation methods under suboptimal conditions. Psychological Methods, 17(3), 354–373. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0029315

 

Mikko

messages.author: bfa43814f6ba1969
messages.subject: Re: Model Identification and Sample Size
parts:
Hi,

 

I cannot recommend any specific literature on that. But it is generally a good idea to estimate smaller and simpler models if your big model does not work. The idea of constraining some parameters based on another model is another general practice. You can see it used in e.g. the SAM modeling approach (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36355708/), but I cannot give you a textbook recommendation on this practice either.

 

The standard, textbook recommendation for your case is to increase the sample size so that you can actually estimate the original model.

 

Mikko
